metadata.note: Janitors and cleaners 2.21M (BLS May 2025), one of the largest US occupations and previously uncovered. Covers chemical safety and never mixing products, restroom sanitation sequence and colour coding, floor care by surface type, waste including sharps and clinical streams, infection control and dwell time, lone working and building security, and the cleaning supervisor and contract manager track.

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and your cleaning or custodial experience.

key_points: Setting first, because the standards are completely different: office, school, hospital or clinic, food production, retail, hotel, industrial plant
Scale in numbers: square footage covered, number of floors or buildings, team size, shift pattern, how many rooms or classrooms per night
What you actually did: general cleaning, floor care including stripping and waxing, carpet extraction, restroom sanitation, waste and recycling, window cleaning, minor maintenance, setup for events
Certifications and training: chemical safety, bloodborne pathogen training, floor equipment, lift or ladder training, infection control if healthcare
One outcome: an inspection score, a building you brought back from a bad state, a route you reorganised, an accident free record
Availability, since most of this work is early morning, evening or overnight
strong_answer_signals: Names the setting, which tells them whether the standards transfer
Gives square footage or room counts rather than only duties
Mentions chemical and equipment training without being asked
avoid: Describing it only as cleaning, with no standards or equipment named
Being vague about shift availability when the work is overnight
No mention of safety training at all

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked without supervision.

key_points: Most of this job is alone or in a small crew at night. That is the real question being asked
Action: how you managed the route, kept to the standard, and paced the shift without anyone checking
Say how you handled finishing early and finishing late, since both are tests of the same thing
Result: the building ready at open, the checklist complete, the inspection passed
Say what you did when nobody would have known if you skipped something
strong_answer_signals: Comfortable and productive working alone
Holds the standard when nobody is watching
Manages pace rather than rushing the end of the shift
avoid: Needing constant direction
A story where the standard slipped because it was late
Suggesting some areas do not need doing if nobody checks

questions.text: Tell me about a difficult cleaning job you handled.

key_points: Options with real difficulty: a flood or leak, a biohazard clean up, a badly neglected area, a post construction clean, a heavy grease kitchen, an infestation aftermath
Action: assess first, get the right protective equipment and chemicals, and know when the job needs a specialist rather than you
Say the method and the order you worked in, since sequence matters in a heavy clean
Result: the state you left it in, the time taken, and any lasting fix such as a repair reported
Say what you reported so the cause was fixed rather than just the mess
strong_answer_signals: Assesses and gets the right equipment before starting
Knows when to call a specialist
Reports the cause, not just the symptom
avoid: Starting a hazardous clean with no protective equipment
Mixing chemicals to make something stronger
Cleaning up a recurring problem repeatedly without ever reporting it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you dealt with a complaint about cleanliness.

key_points: Situation: who complained and what about. Often the complaint is about a recurring area rather than one bad night
Action: look at it yourself rather than defending, fix it immediately if you can, and be honest if it was missed
Find out why: time pressure, an area not on the route, a broken machine, a supply shortage, or a genuine miss
Tell the supervisor so the route or the schedule is corrected rather than the same complaint returning
Result: the area fixed and the complaint not repeated
strong_answer_signals: Looks at it before defending
Finds the cause rather than just cleaning it again
Honest when it was genuinely missed
avoid: Arguing that it was clean when you left
Blaming the previous shift
Fixing the same complaint every week without reporting it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found something you had to report.

key_points: Options: a water leak, an electrical fault, a broken lock or window, a fire door propped open, a sharps or biohazard find, evidence of a break in, someone in the building who should not be there
Action: what you did immediately to make it safe, and who you told
Say why you did not just deal with it yourself when it was outside your scope
Result: the risk removed, the repair made, the incident recorded
Custodians are often the only person in a building at night. Say that you take that responsibility seriously
strong_answer_signals: Makes it safe first, then reports
Knows what is outside their scope
Understands they are often the only person in the building
avoid: Ignoring a fault because it is not your job
Handling an electrical or structural problem yourself
Waiting until the next day to report a security issue

questions.text: Tell me about working as part of a cleaning team.

key_points: Say how the work was split: by area, by task, or by floor, and how handovers worked
Action: what you did when a colleague was absent or fell behind, and how you communicated across a shift
Say how you kept the shared equipment and store room in a state the next person could use
Result: the building covered, the standard held, and the shift finished together
Small crews at night depend on each other. Show that you are the person people want on the shift
strong_answer_signals: Covers for a colleague without being asked
Leaves equipment and stores usable for the next person
Communicates across shifts
avoid: Leaving the store room or machines in a poor state
Finishing your area and sitting down while others work
A story that is mostly about a colleague not pulling their weight

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to work around people using the building.

key_points: Settings where this matters: a school during the day, an office with staff working late, a hospital ward, a retail floor with customers
Action: minimise disruption. Signage for wet floors, quiet equipment where possible, working around people politely, timing the loud jobs
Say how you interact: greet people, answer politely, and know what you can and cannot discuss about the building
Safety first: never leave a wet floor unsigned or a cable across a walkway
Result: the work done with no complaints and no incidents
strong_answer_signals: Signs and protects the area every time
Times disruptive work deliberately
Professional and pleasant with occupants
avoid: Mopping a busy corridor with no signage
Running loud equipment during a class or a meeting
Treating occupants as an obstacle

questions.text: Tell me about a mistake you made at work.

key_points: Real examples: using the wrong chemical on a surface, damaging a floor finish, breaking something while moving it, missing an area, setting an alarm off
Own it and report it immediately. A damaged surface reported is a repair, and one hidden is a bigger bill
Action: what you did to limit the damage and who you told
Result and the habit that changed, such as reading the label or checking the surface first
If it involved a chemical or a safety issue, say plainly why hiding it was never an option
strong_answer_signals: Reports immediately rather than hoping
Names the specific habit change
Treats chemical and safety mistakes as a separate category
avoid: Saying you have never made one
Hiding damage to a floor or a surface
Blaming the label or the supervisor

questions.text: Tell me about feedback you received from a supervisor.

key_points: Real feedback here: missed areas, restroom detail, streaking on glass or floors, time management on the route, chemical use, not signing the checklist
Action: how you asked what the standard was and what you practised
Result: the inspection score, the complaint that stopped, the route completed on time
Say whether you asked for a walk through with the supervisor, since that is the fastest way to learn a standard
strong_answer_signals: Asks for a walk through to see the standard
Practises the specific thing
Evidence the change held
avoid: Feedback that was really praise
Disagreeing with the standard
No evidence anything changed

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to finish a large job in a short window.

key_points: Situations: a school between terms, an office move, an event turnaround, a deep clean before an inspection
Action: plan the sequence, gather the equipment and supplies first, and work the areas in an order that avoids redoing work
Say how you asked for help or extra hours early rather than at the end
Say what you protected: the visible areas and the health critical areas such as restrooms and food areas
Result: finished on time, with the numbers if you have them
strong_answer_signals: Plans the sequence so nothing gets redone
Asks for help early
Protects restrooms and food areas as the priority
avoid: Working faster by skipping the restrooms
Not asking for help until the deadline passed
No plan, just working harder

questions.text: What do you know about cleaning chemicals and safety?

key_points: Read the label and follow the dilution. Stronger is not better, it damages surfaces and it is a health risk
Never mix chemicals. Bleach with ammonia or with acid produces toxic gas, and this is the answer they are listening for
Know where the safety data sheets are and that you are entitled to read them
Use the right protective equipment: gloves, eye protection, and ventilation for anything strong
Store correctly: labelled containers, never in a drink bottle, chemicals away from food, and locked where the public or children can reach
Dwell time matters. A disinfectant that is wiped off immediately has not disinfected anything
strong_answer_signals: Says never mix chemicals and names why
Knows dwell time is required for disinfection
Knows where the safety data sheets are
avoid: Mixing products to make something stronger
Decanting a chemical into an unlabelled bottle
Treating a disinfectant as a wipe and go product

questions.text: How do you clean and sanitise a restroom properly?

key_points: Restrooms decide how a building is judged. Say that up front, because it is true
Work top down and clean to dirty: mirrors and dispensers, then sinks and counters, then fixtures, then floors last
Use separate cloths or a colour coded system so a toilet cloth never touches a sink. Cross contamination is the whole risk here
Apply the disinfectant and leave the dwell time before wiping
Restock everything: soap, paper, sanitiser, and check the hand dryers
Finish with the detail people notice: door handles, light switches, the underside of fixtures, the floor edges and corners
Sign the check sheet honestly and record anything broken
strong_answer_signals: Top down and clean to dirty
Colour coded cloths to prevent cross contamination
Details: handles, switches, floor edges
avoid: Using the same cloth on toilets and sinks
Signing a check sheet for work not done
Leaving dispensers empty

questions.text: What do you know about floor care?

key_points: Match the method to the floor type: vinyl, sealed concrete, terrazzo, ceramic, wood, laminate, and carpet all need different products
Daily care is dust mopping or vacuuming first, then damp mopping. Mopping over grit grinds the finish off a floor
Change the mop water when it is dirty. A dirty bucket spreads soil rather than removing it
Periodic work: scrubbing, stripping and refinishing, burnishing, and carpet extraction. Say which you have done and on what equipment
Never put water on a wood floor or a strong alkaline product on a surface that cannot take it
Safety: wet floor signs, work in sections so there is always a dry route, and never leave a stripped floor unattended
strong_answer_signals: Knows dust mopping comes before wet mopping and why
Matches product to floor type
Works in sections so there is a dry route
avoid: Wet mopping without sweeping first
Using the same product on every floor type
Blocking a whole corridor with a wet floor

questions.text: How do you handle waste and recycling?

key_points: Separate correctly at source: general, recycling, organic, confidential paper, and hazardous or clinical where the site has it
Never mix clinical or hazardous waste into general waste. That is a regulatory issue, not a housekeeping preference
Handle sharps only with the correct container and never by hand. In healthcare and in public buildings this is a real risk
Bag properly, do not overfill, and never press a bag down with your hand or foot
Keep the bin store clean and the routes clear, since that is where pests start
Report contamination in the recycling stream rather than sending it all to landfill silently
strong_answer_signals: Never handles sharps by hand
Knows clinical and hazardous waste is regulated
Never compresses a bag by hand
avoid: Pressing down a bag that could contain glass or a needle
Mixing clinical waste into general
Overfilling bags to save trips

questions.text: What equipment can you operate?

key_points: Name what you have actually run: vacuum types, auto scrubber, floor buffer or burnisher, carpet extractor, pressure washer, wet vacuum, powered sweeper
Say whether you have training or certification for anything requiring it, such as a lift or a ride on machine
Daily care: check before use, empty and clean after use, change pads and filters, and report faults rather than working around them
Never use a machine you have not been trained on. A floor buffer in untrained hands causes injuries
Battery and cord safety: cords across walkways, wet areas, and charging in a ventilated space
Say what you do when a machine fails mid shift
strong_answer_signals: Honest about training on each machine
Cleans and checks equipment as routine
Refuses to run untrained equipment
avoid: Claiming experience on a machine you have watched
Running a machine with a damaged cord
Leaving equipment dirty for the next shift

questions.text: How do you work to a cleaning schedule or specification?

key_points: Know the difference between daily, weekly, monthly and periodic tasks. A specification exists so nothing is quietly dropped
Work a route in a consistent order so nothing is missed and the time is predictable
Record what was done honestly, since the signed record is what the client sees
Flag when the schedule does not fit reality: an area that needs more, a task nobody has time for, a room that is always locked
Adjust for the building: exam weeks, flu season, winter salt and mud, an event, a construction area
Say how long your route takes and how you know
strong_answer_signals: Follows a consistent route order
Signs records honestly
Flags when the spec does not match reality
avoid: Signing off tasks not done
Dropping periodic work quietly because nobody notices for months
Never raising an area that consistently cannot be covered

questions.text: What do you know about infection control?

key_points: Understand what you are actually doing: cleaning removes soil, disinfecting kills organisms, and you must clean before you disinfect
High touch points are the priority: door handles, light switches, handrails, lift buttons, taps, shared keyboards and phones, desks
Dwell time and correct dilution, since both are what make a disinfectant work
Colour coded equipment by area so nothing moves from a restroom to a kitchen
Hand hygiene and gloves used correctly. Gloves are not a substitute for washing hands and they get changed between areas
In healthcare or during an outbreak, follow the enhanced protocol exactly and never improvise
strong_answer_signals: Clean before disinfect, stated correctly
Names high touch points as the priority
Colour coding between areas
avoid: Spraying and wiping immediately
Using the same cloth from a restroom in a kitchen
Treating gloves as a replacement for hand washing

questions.text: What health and safety rules apply to your work?

key_points: Wet floors: signs out before you start, work in sections, remove signs when dry so people do not learn to ignore them
Manual handling: lift with your legs, get help for heavy items, use a trolley, and never carry more than you can see over
Ladders and heights: use the right equipment, never a chair, and follow the site rule on working alone at height
Chemical safety, protective equipment, and knowing the emergency eyewash location
Electrical safety: check cords, keep them out of walkways, and never use damaged equipment
Report every injury and near miss, however small. The record is what changes the process
Lone working procedure: check in, check out, and a plan if you do not
strong_answer_signals: Removes signs when dry, which shows real understanding
Reports near misses, not just injuries
Knows the lone working procedure
avoid: Standing on a chair or a desk to reach
Leaving wet floor signs out permanently
Not reporting a minor injury

questions.text: How do you manage supplies and stock?

key_points: Know your usage so you order before you run out rather than after. Running out of paper or soap is the complaint that reaches management fastest
Store correctly: chemicals secured and labelled, paper goods dry, nothing blocking an exit or a sprinkler head
Use the correct dilution rather than pouring generously. Over dilution is one of the biggest cost lines in this work
Rotate stock and keep the store room organised so anyone can find things
Report waste and theft, and keep the store locked where policy requires it
Say what you did that reduced cost or waste
strong_answer_signals: Orders on usage rather than when empty
Correct dilution framed as a cost control
Keeps the store room usable for others
avoid: Free pouring chemicals
Blocking exits or sprinkler heads with stock
Leaving a chemical store unlocked in a public building

questions.text: What minor maintenance can you do?

key_points: Say honestly what you are comfortable and permitted to do: changing light tubes where allowed, unblocking a sink, replacing a dispenser, tightening a fitting, minor painting, salting a path
Know the line clearly: electrical work, gas, structural, roof work, and anything requiring a licence goes to a qualified person
Report faults with enough detail that the trade arrives with the right part
Do the preventive things that stop bigger problems: clearing gutters and drains where safe, checking for leaks, keeping vents clear
Log everything so the building has a history
Say that doing an unqualified repair is a liability, not helpfulness
strong_answer_signals: Clear about the line between minor and licensed work
Reports faults with useful detail
Does preventive checks
avoid: Attempting electrical or gas work
Reporting a fault as something is broken with no detail
Repeatedly patching a problem instead of reporting it

questions.text: How do you handle building security as part of your job?

key_points: You are often the only person in the building. Locking up properly is part of the work, not an afterthought
Follow the procedure: check the building before setting the alarm, secure doors and windows, do not prop fire doors, and do not share codes or keys
Challenge politely or report anyone in the building who should not be there. Never confront someone who could be dangerous
Know the emergency procedure: alarm activation, fire, medical emergency, and who to call
Protect what you see. Offices, records and personal belongings are confidential even when they are left out
Report anything unusual: a forced door, an unfamiliar vehicle, an alarm that failed to set
strong_answer_signals: Treats keys and codes as a trust responsibility
Reports rather than confronting
Understands confidentiality of what they see
avoid: Sharing alarm codes or keys
Propping a fire door for convenience
Confronting an intruder alone

questions.text: How is your work measured?

key_points: Inspection scores or audits against the specification, which is the most common measure
Complaints received, and more importantly repeat complaints about the same area
Route completion within the shift, and whether periodic tasks are actually being done
Supply cost per square foot or per month, which is where dilution discipline shows up
Safety record: incidents, near misses, and days without an accident
Say which of these you personally influenced and by how much
strong_answer_signals: Knows inspections are scored against a specification
Distinguishes a complaint from a repeat complaint
Connects dilution discipline to cost
avoid: Thinking the job is unmeasurable
No awareness of the inspection process
Never having seen the specification for their own area

questions.text: You find a spill of an unknown substance. What do you do?

key_points: Do not touch it or clean it until you know what it is. That is the whole answer
Secure the area first: signs, a barrier, and keep people away
Try to identify it: a nearby container, a label, or ask someone who works in that area
For a chemical spill, follow the spill procedure and the safety data sheet, and use the spill kit if you are trained on it
For blood or body fluid, use the biohazard procedure, full protective equipment, and the correct disinfectant and disposal
Report it and record it, and never dispose of an unknown chemical down a drain
strong_answer_signals: Secures the area before doing anything else
Identifies before cleaning
Knows the biohazard and chemical spill procedures are different
avoid: Mopping up something unidentified
Pouring an unknown chemical down a drain
Cleaning blood with no protective equipment

questions.text: Someone asks you to let them into a locked room. What do you do?

key_points: Politely decline unless you have been authorised. Being helpful is not worth the risk here
Verify: who they are, whether they are on the authorised list, and whether you can confirm it with a supervisor or security
Explain the procedure rather than treating them as a suspect. Most requests are genuine and people understand a rule applied consistently
Offer the route: contact their manager, security, or come back when someone with authority can confirm
Report it if the request was persistent or if something felt wrong
Say that access rules exist to protect you as much as the building
strong_answer_signals: Declines politely without authorisation
Offers a route rather than a flat refusal
Reports a persistent or odd request
avoid: Letting someone in because they seemed senior or in a hurry
Deciding on your own who looks legitimate
Not reporting a suspicious request

questions.text: You cannot finish your route in the time available. What do you do?

key_points: Prioritise properly: health critical first, which is restrooms, food areas, and high touch points. Then visible and high traffic areas. Then the rest
Tell the supervisor during the shift, not after. They can move someone or adjust the plan
Record honestly what was not done rather than signing it off
Say if the route is consistently too big, with the timings to back it up
Never skip the restrooms to make the route fit. That is the area everyone judges the building by
strong_answer_signals: Health critical areas first
Tells the supervisor during the shift
Records honestly what was missed
avoid: Signing off the whole route regardless
Skipping restrooms to save time
Complaining about the workload without providing timings

questions.text: A staff member is rude to you about the cleaning. What do you do?

key_points: Stay professional. Listen to what the actual complaint is under the tone
If they are right, say so simply and fix it. If it was not your area or your shift, say that without blaming a colleague by name
Do not argue and do not accept abuse. Tell your supervisor if it becomes personal or repeated
Report the substance of the complaint so it gets fixed properly
Say plainly that you are entitled to be treated respectfully and that there is a process for it
strong_answer_signals: Separates the complaint from the tone
Fixes it if they are right
Reports abuse rather than absorbing it
avoid: Arguing back
Naming a colleague as the person who failed
Accepting abuse because of the job title

questions.text: You find a wallet or a phone while cleaning. What do you do?

key_points: Do not open it, do not use it, and do not take it home for safekeeping
Follow the lost property procedure exactly: hand it to security or the supervisor and record it with the time and the location found
Get a receipt or make sure it is logged, since that record protects you
For cash or valuables, get a second person present when you hand it over where the policy allows
Say plainly that this is a trust question and that the record is what protects everyone
strong_answer_signals: Logs it with time and location
Wants a second person or a record for valuables
Never opens or keeps it
avoid: Putting it in your locker to hand in later
Opening a wallet to find out whose it is
Handing it to a colleague informally with no record

questions.text: You are asked to use a chemical you have not been trained on. What do you do?

key_points: Ask for the safety data sheet and the training before using it. You are entitled to both
Check the label for dilution, protective equipment, ventilation, and surface compatibility
Say that you will not use a product you do not understand, calmly and without making it a confrontation
Ask your supervisor to show you or to assign someone trained
Report if you are pressured to use something unsafely
Say that chemical injuries and damaged surfaces are both permanent and both avoidable
strong_answer_signals: Asks for the safety data sheet
Declines calmly rather than refusing aggressively
Reports pressure to use something unsafely
avoid: Using it and hoping
Guessing at dilution
Trying it on a surface to see what happens

questions.text: You notice a colleague not following procedure. What do you do?

key_points: Say something directly and quietly first. Most of it is habit rather than defiance
Be specific: mixing chemicals, skipping protective equipment, not signing records, propping fire doors, using the wrong cloth in a restroom
Escalate to a supervisor if it continues or if it is a safety or infection control issue
Frame it as protecting the building and the team rather than reporting someone
Say that anything involving chemicals, biohazard or fire safety goes up immediately, not after a second chance
strong_answer_signals: Addresses it directly first
Escalates safety issues immediately
Frames it around the risk, not the person
avoid: Saying nothing because it is awkward
Reporting it to everyone except the supervisor
Giving a second chance on a chemical or fire safety breach

questions.text: There is a burst pipe or flood in the building overnight. What do you do?

key_points: Safety first: if water is near electrics, do not enter. Isolate power only if you are trained and it is safe
Stop the source if you know where the stop valve is and it is safe to reach
Call the emergency contact and the supervisor immediately. This is not a job to handle alone and then mention in the morning
Contain and protect: barriers, wet vacuum, move what you safely can, protect equipment and records
Sign the area and keep people out
Document with photographs, since insurance and the repair both depend on it
strong_answer_signals: Recognises the electrical risk first
Calls immediately rather than handling it alone
Photographs for the insurance record
avoid: Wading into standing water near electrics
Cleaning it up and reporting it the next day
Not photographing the damage

questions.text: A parent, student or member of the public asks you a question about the building. What do you do?

key_points: Be helpful and polite. In a school or a public building you are part of the impression the place makes
Answer what you know: directions, opening times, where to find the office
Do not answer what you do not know or what is not yours to share: staff whereabouts, student information, security arrangements, or anything confidential
Direct them to the office or the right person rather than guessing
In a school, follow the safeguarding rules on interacting with children and report any concern through the proper route
Report anything that felt wrong rather than deciding it was probably nothing
strong_answer_signals: Helpful within their scope
Does not share information that is not theirs to share
Knows the safeguarding route in a school
avoid: Guessing at an answer
Discussing staff or student matters
Deciding on your own that a concern was probably nothing

questions.text: An inspection or audit is happening tomorrow. What do you do?

key_points: The honest answer is that a building ready for inspection is a building cleaned properly all year. Say that first
Check the specification and walk your area looking at it as an inspector would, from the entrance rather than from your usual position
Focus on what is actually scored: restrooms, high touch points, floor edges and corners, glass, dispensers stocked, records complete
Fix the things you have been meaning to report, and report the ones you cannot fix
Make sure the records and check sheets are complete and honest
Say what you would do afterwards with any finding: correct it and change the routine so it holds
strong_answer_signals: Says continuous readiness is the real answer
Looks at the area from the visitor viewpoint
Corrects the routine after a finding, not just the fault
avoid: A frantic clean the night before as the whole plan
Backfilling check sheets to look complete
Fixing the finding without changing the routine

questions.text: How do you supervise a cleaning team?

key_points: Make the standard visible: a written specification, a walk through, and photographs of what good looks like. Most failures are unclear expectations
Build routes that actually fit the time. A route nobody can finish teaches the team to sign off work they did not do
Be present on the floor, including on the night shift. A supervisor who never sees the overnight work does not know the building
Inspect regularly and consistently, and give feedback the same night rather than in a monthly meeting
Cover absence with a plan rather than by overloading whoever turned up
Recognise good work specifically. This is a job where people are noticed only when something is wrong
strong_answer_signals: Routes that fit the time available
Sees the night shift
Recognises good work, not only failures
avoid: Managing entirely from inspection reports
Routes that cannot be completed
Only speaking to the team when there is a complaint

questions.text: How do you handle a client or building manager complaint?

key_points: Go and look at it yourself before responding. Never defend an area you have not seen
Acknowledge it plainly and give a time for the fix rather than an explanation first
Find the cause: the route, the schedule, a machine, a supply issue, training, or a genuine performance problem
Fix the underlying cause and tell the client what changed. A complaint that returns is far more damaging than the first one
Track repeat complaints by area, since the pattern is the real information
Support the cleaner privately while still fixing the problem
strong_answer_signals: Looks before responding
Fixes the cause and reports the change
Tracks repeat complaints by area
avoid: Defending the team before checking
Blaming the cleaner to the client
Fixing the same complaint repeatedly without changing anything

questions.text: How do you plan staffing and routes for a building?

key_points: Start from the specification and the actual areas: square footage, floor types, room counts, and the frequency each task needs
Use realistic production rates rather than guesses, and time a route before committing to it
Build in the periodic work rather than assuming it happens in spare time. It never does
Schedule around the building: when it is occupied, when the loud work can happen, when access is possible
Plan for absence with a cover arrangement rather than assuming full attendance
Review after a month against reality and adjust rather than blaming the team for the plan
strong_answer_signals: Times a route before committing
Schedules periodic work explicitly
Reviews the plan against reality
avoid: Building a route from a spreadsheet and never walking it
Assuming periodic work fits in spare time
Blaming the team when the plan was wrong

questions.text: How do you control supply and equipment costs?

key_points: Dilution control is the biggest single lever. Dispensing systems and training beat telling people to use less
Track usage per building and per month so an anomaly is visible rather than absorbed
Standardise products rather than carrying twenty. Fewer products means better training and better pricing
Maintain equipment properly. A machine that fails costs more in labour than the maintenance would have
Review contracts and get comparative pricing rather than renewing by habit
Never cut consumables that occupants see, such as paper and soap. That saving costs the contract
strong_answer_signals: Dilution systems rather than instructions
Tracks usage per building
Refuses to cut visible consumables
avoid: Cutting paper and soap to hit a budget
Carrying dozens of products
Deferring machine maintenance

questions.text: How do you handle a team member whose work is below standard?

key_points: Check the standard is actually clear before treating it as performance. Show, do not just tell
Diagnose: training, equipment, an unrealistic route, a health issue, or genuine effort. They need different responses
Walk the area with them and agree what good looks like, then set a review date and keep it
Document fairly and follow the process if it does not improve, consistently for everyone
Act on it. A team notices immediately when someone is carried and it damages everyone else
Say what you did that turned someone around, since that is the answer they want
strong_answer_signals: Checks the standard is clear first
Walks the area with them
Acts rather than tolerating
avoid: Warnings without a walk through
Applying standards inconsistently
Letting it continue because staff are hard to replace

questions.text: How do you manage health and safety for a cleaning team?

key_points: Training first and recorded: chemicals, manual handling, equipment, working at height, lone working
Safety data sheets accessible where the chemicals are, not in an office nobody visits
Protective equipment provided, correct, and actually available rather than requested
Investigate every incident and near miss for the cause. Slips, manual handling and chemical exposure are the big three
Lone working procedure with check in and check out, because most of this work happens when the building is empty
Make it clear that a task can be stopped for safety and that nobody is penalised for it
strong_answer_signals: Names slips, manual handling and chemicals as the big three
Lone working procedure taken seriously
Supports stopping a task for safety
avoid: Training that is not recorded
Protective equipment that has to be requested
Only investigating incidents that caused injury

questions.text: How do you keep staff in a high turnover job?

key_points: Start with what people actually leave over: unrealistic routes, being spoken to badly, unpredictable hours, and equipment that does not work
Train properly at the start. Most early leavers were never shown the standard
Give predictable shifts and publish rotas early
Provide the tools. Nothing demoralises a cleaner faster than a broken machine and a mop that does not clean
Recognise people by name and in front of the client where you can. This work is invisible until it fails
Create a path: trainer, team lead, supervisor, floor care specialist
Give the number: turnover or average tenure
strong_answer_signals: Names routes and equipment as retention issues
Fixes onboarding
Makes the work visible to the client
avoid: Treating turnover as unavoidable
Relying on pay alone
Ignoring broken equipment as a morale issue

questions.text: How do you win or keep a cleaning contract?

key_points: Know the building and price it honestly. A contract won by underpricing fails on quality within three months
Show the specification, the frequencies, and the staffing that delivers it, so the client can see what they are buying
Be reachable and responsive. Most contracts are lost on communication, not on cleaning
Report proactively: audit scores, completed periodic work, issues found in the building
Handle problems visibly. A client who sees a problem fixed quickly trusts you more than one who never sees a problem
Add value the client notices: reporting maintenance faults, flagging security issues, adjusting for their busy periods
strong_answer_signals: Prices honestly rather than to win
Reports proactively rather than when asked
Understands contracts are lost on communication
avoid: Underpricing to win and cutting hours later
Only contacting the client when invoicing
Hiding a service failure rather than reporting it

questions.text: Why do you want this job?

key_points: Give an honest reason: you like finishing a shift and seeing the result, you prefer working independently, the hours suit you, you take pride in a building looking right
Connect it to something you have actually done
Say what you are good at: thoroughness, reliability, working alone, physical stamina
Practical reasons such as hours and location are respected here when paired with genuine commitment
strong_answer_signals: An honest reason rather than a rehearsed one
Names what they are actually good at
Comfortable with the practical motivations
avoid: Only saying you need a job
Suggesting the work is beneath you
Nothing about standards or pride in the work

questions.text: How do you feel about working nights or early mornings?

key_points: Be exact and honest. Most of this work happens when the building is empty and a vague answer becomes a problem in week two
Say how you manage it: sleep routine, transport, and whether you have done it before
State any genuine constraint up front: transport at night, caring responsibilities, a second job
Say what you like about it if you do, such as working without interruption
strong_answer_signals: Exact about availability
Has actually done the shift pattern or knows what it takes
States constraints up front
avoid: Saying you are flexible when you are not
Discovering a transport problem after starting
Complaining about the hours in the interview

questions.text: What does a good job look like to you?

key_points: Describe it concretely: restrooms you would use yourself, floors with no streaks or edges missed, dispensers full, bins empty, nothing sticky, nothing missed in the corners
Say that the test is walking back in from the entrance and looking at it as someone arriving would
Mention the invisible part: high touch points, and the areas nobody checks
Say that consistency is the real standard. A good night and a bad night is not a standard
strong_answer_signals: Describes it concretely rather than saying clean
Checks from the visitor viewpoint
Values consistency over one good night
avoid: Saying you just clean everything
No mention of restrooms or detail areas
Defining good as whatever passes

questions.text: How do you handle the physical demands?

key_points: Be straightforward. This is physical work: standing, walking, lifting, bending, repetitive movement, for a full shift
Say how you manage it: technique on lifting, using equipment rather than carrying, pacing the route, footwear, breaks
Say that reporting a strain early is better than working through it, since back injuries end careers in this trade
Be honest about anything you cannot do, since discovering it later helps nobody
strong_answer_signals: Realistic about the physical demand
Uses equipment rather than carrying
Reports strain early
avoid: Claiming you can lift anything
Working through an injury as a point of pride
Hiding a physical limitation until it becomes a problem

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in a couple of years?

key_points: Honest options here: staying and being excellent at it, floor care specialist, team lead, supervisor, contract manager, or moving into building maintenance
If you want to stay in the role, say so. It is a legitimate answer and employers value people who mean it
Name what you would need to learn for whatever step you want, such as floor machine training or a supervisor course
Show you intend to do this job well regardless
strong_answer_signals: Comfortable saying they want to stay and be good at it
Names a specific step and what it needs
Committed to the current role either way
avoid: Claiming ambitions you do not have
Making clear this is temporary until something better
No thought about it

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?

key_points: Ask what tells you what the job actually is:
"What area or route would I cover, and how long is it expected to take?"
"How many people are on a shift and is there a supervisor on site?"
"What equipment and products are provided, and what condition are they in?"
"Is there training on the machines and the chemicals?"
"How is the work inspected, and how often?"
The route size against the shift length is the question that decides whether the job is doable
strong_answer_signals: Asks about route size against shift length
Asks about equipment condition and training
Asks how the work is inspected
avoid: No questions
Only asking about pay
Asking something already covered
